questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-8\lambda {y}^{′}+16{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,y(0)=0,\,y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=0$ and $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-8\lambda m+16{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-4\lambda )(m-4\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=4\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{4\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{4\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{4\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A+B\cdot 0=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=Bx{e}^{4\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′}=B{e}^{4\lambda x}+4B\lambda x{e}^{4\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}B{e}^{4\lambda }+B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ 2B{e}^{4\lambda }+4B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }+2B\lambda {e}^{4\lambda } & =0 \\ B{e}^{4\lambda }(1+2\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require $B\ne 0.$ Thus, since ${e}^{4\lambda }>0,$ we must have

$$
\lambda =-\frac{1}{2}.
$$

Therefore, the corresponding eigenfunction is

$$
\begin{aligned}y(x) & =Bx{e}^{4\lambda x} \\  & =Bx{e}^{-2x}.\end{aligned}
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-10\lambda {y}^{′}+25{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0,\,1\le x\le 2,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ and $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-10\lambda m+25{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-5\lambda )(m-5\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=5\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{5\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{5\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{5\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{5\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda x}+B{e}^{5\lambda x}+5B\lambda x{e}^{5\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}5A\lambda {e}^{5\lambda }+B{e}^{5\lambda }+5B\lambda {e}^{5\lambda } & =0 \\ 5A\lambda +B+5B\lambda  & =0 \\ (5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(2)+2{y}^{′}(2)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{10\lambda }+2B{e}^{10\lambda }+2(5A\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }+B{e}^{10\lambda }+10B\lambda {e}^{10\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+2B+2(5A\lambda +B+10B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+2B+10A\lambda +2B+20B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+(4+20\lambda )B & =0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0 \\ (1+10\lambda )A+4(1+5\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}5\lambda  & 1+5\lambda  \\ 1+10\lambda  & 4(1+5\lambda )\end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}5\lambda \cdot 4(1+5\lambda )-(1+5\lambda )(1+10\lambda ) & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -(1+10\lambda )] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )[20\lambda -1-10\lambda ] & =0 \\ (1+5\lambda )(10\lambda -1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{5}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+(1-1)B=0
$$

 
which gives $A=0,$ and where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=Bx{e}^{-x}.
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{10},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{5{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(5\lambda )A+(1+5\lambda )B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+\frac{3}{2}B=0\,⇒\,A=-3B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-3B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-3) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-3)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $Bx{e}^{-x}\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-3).$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}-12\lambda {y}^{′}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0,\,0\le x\le 1,\,\lambda \in R.
$$

Find the eigenvalues and eigenfunctions of this problem. Assume that $B$ and $C$ are constants.

$\,$ The eigenvalues are $\lambda =$ {{field-1}}.

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are $y=$ {{field-2}}.
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ is not an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda \ne 0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}-12\lambda m+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0 \\ (m-6\lambda )(m-6\lambda ) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the double root $m=6\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)={e}^{6\lambda x},\,{y}_{2}(x)=x{e}^{6\lambda x}
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A{e}^{6\lambda x}+Bx{e}^{6\lambda x}.
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}^{′} & =6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda x}+B{e}^{6\lambda x}+6B\lambda x{e}^{6\lambda x}.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}6A\lambda +B & =0 \\ (6\lambda )A+B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(1)+2{y}^{′}(1)=0$ yields

$$
\begin{aligned}A{e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+2(6A\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }+B{e}^{6\lambda }+6B\lambda {e}^{6\lambda }) & =0 \\ A+B+2(6A\lambda +B+6B\lambda ) & =0 \\ A+B+12A\lambda +2B+12B\lambda  & =0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have the following systems of equations for $A$ and $B:$

$$
\{\begin{aligned}(6\lambda )A+B=0 \\ (1+12\lambda )A+(3+12\lambda )B=0\end{aligned}
$$

This homogeneous linear system has a nontrivial solution if and only if the determinant is zero. This gives

$$
|\begin{aligned}6\lambda  & 1 \\ 1+12\lambda  & 3+12\lambda \end{aligned}|=0.
$$

So, we get

$$
\begin{aligned}6\lambda (3+12\lambda )-(1)(1+12\lambda ) & =0 \\ 18\lambda +72{\lambda }^{2}-1-12\lambda  & =0 \\ 72{\lambda }^{2}+6\lambda -1 & =0 \\ (12\lambda -1)(6\lambda +1) & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

Thus, we have the eigenvalues ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}\text{ and }{\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12}.$

Finally, we find the eigenfunction corresponding to each eigenvalue:

- Consider ${\lambda }_{1}=-\frac{1}{6}.$ Then, we have the solution

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{1}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{1}x} \\  & =A{e}^{-x}+Bx{e}^{-x}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{1}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
-A+B=0\,⇒\,A=B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=B{e}^{-x}(x+1).
$$

- For ${\lambda }_{2}=\frac{1}{12},$ we have

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =A{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x}+Bx{e}^{6{\lambda }_{2}x} \\  & =A{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2}\end{aligned}
$$

and substituting ${\lambda }_{2}$ into

$$
(6\lambda )A+B=0
$$

 
we get 

$$
\frac{1}{2}A+B=0\,⇒\,A=-2B
$$

where $B$ is a free parameter. Thus, the eigenfunction corresponding to this eigenvalue is

$$
\begin{aligned}{y}_{2}(x) & =-2B{e}^{x/2}+Bx{e}^{x/2} \\  & =B{e}^{x/2}(x-2) \\  & =C{e}^{x/2}(x-2)\end{aligned}
$$

where we have set $C=B.$

So, the eigenfunctions corresponding to ${\lambda }_{1}$ and ${\lambda }_{2},$ respectively, are $B{e}^{-x}(x+1)\text{ and }C{e}^{x/2}(x-2).$

Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+36{\lambda }^{2}y=0,\,{y}^{′}(0)=0,\,y(3)=0,\,0\le x\le 3,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda \ne 0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ and $y(3)=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+36{\lambda }^{2} & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 6\text{i}\lambda .$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x)
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Differentiating gives

$$
{y}^{′}=-6A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(6\lambda x)+6B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition ${y}^{′}(0)=0$ yields

$$
-6A\lambda \operatorname{sin}⁡(0)+6B\lambda \operatorname{cos}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $B=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(6\lambda x).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(3)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(18\lambda )=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
18\lambda =\frac{\pi }{2}+n\pi =\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{2}
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{(2n+1)\pi }{36}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{cos}⁡(6{\lambda }_{n}x),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
$$

questions.problem:
Consider the boundary value problem

$$
{y}^{″}+16\lambda y=0,\,y(0)=y(\pi )=0,\,0\le x\le \pi ,\,\lambda \ge 0.
$$

Find the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues and the associated eigenfunctions of this problem.

$\,$ The eigenvalues correspond to the parameter values ${\lambda }_{n}=$ {{field-1}}, where $n\in N.$

$\,$ The eigenfunctions are ${y}_{n}(x)=$ {{field-2}}, where ${B}_{n}\in R.$
questions.worked_solution:
We consider the cases $\lambda =0$ and $\lambda >0$ separately, since they correspond to different solutions. 

**Case 1**: First, we consider $\lambda =0.$ 

Setting $\lambda =0$ gives the equation

$$
{y}^{″}=0.
$$

Integrating this equation gives

$$
y=Ax+B.
$$

Applying the conditions $y(0)=y(\pi )=0$ yields the trivial solution $y≡0.$ Since the zero solution is not an eigenfunction, $\lambda =0$ does not correspond to an eigenvalue.

**Case 2**: Next, we consider $\lambda >0.$

To find the fundamental solutions, we set $y={e}^{mx}.$ The auxiliary equation is

$$
\begin{aligned}{m}^{2}+16\lambda  & =0.\end{aligned}
$$

So, we have $m=\pm 4\text{i}\sqrt{\lambda }.$ So, the fundamental solutions are 

$$
{y}_{1}(x)=\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }),\,{y}_{2}(x)=\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda })
$$

and the general solution is

$$
y=A\operatorname{cos}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda })+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(0)=0$ yields

$$
A\operatorname{cos}⁡(0)+B\operatorname{sin}⁡(0)=0
$$

which gives $A=0.$ So, we have

$$
y=B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{\lambda }).
$$

Applying the boundary condition $y(\pi )=0$ yields

$$
B\operatorname{sin}⁡(4\pi \sqrt{\lambda })=0.
$$

For nontrivial solutions, we require 

$$
4\pi \sqrt{\lambda }=n\pi 
$$

for $n\in N.$ This gives the parameter values corresponding to the eigenvalues:

$$
{\lambda }_{n}=\frac{{n}^{2}}{16}.
$$

The corresponding eigenfunctions are 

$$
{y}_{n}(x)={B}_{n}\operatorname{sin}⁡(4x\sqrt{{\lambda }_{n}}),\,{B}_{n}\in R.
